slides.text:
Welcome to Module 10, Reshaping Data in PostgreSQL.

[pause=0.7]

Reshaping changes structure, not the underlying facts.

[pause=0.7]

We will move between long and wide forms, pivot categories into columns, unpivot columns back into rows, preserve meaningful NULL values, and protect the intended analytical grain.

[pause=0.7]

The most important habit in this module is to say what one output row represents before you write the reshape query.

[pause=1.0]

Long and wide are not quality levels.

[pause=0.7]

They are different ways to arrange information.

[pause=0.7]

Long data usually stores categories as row values.

[pause=0.7]

Wide data turns selected category values into columns.

[pause=0.7]

The dangerous part is that many pivots also aggregate.

[pause=0.7]

When several source rows map to one pivot cell, detail may be permanently removed.

[pause=1.0]

By the end of this module, you should be able to identify long and wide structures, pivot and unpivot data in PostgreSQL, and explain the grain of each result.

[pause=0.7]

You should also be able to detect when a reshape changes more than structure because aggregation or a join has altered the facts.

[pause=0.7]

Finally, you should be able to choose a shape based on what happens next: visualization, reporting, or modeling.

[pause=1.0]

The module starts with the shape itself.

[pause=0.7]

Then we will pivot long data to wide form.

[pause=0.7]

After that, we will unpivot wide data back to long form.

[pause=0.7]

Next comes the most important safeguard: grain.

[pause=0.7]

Finally, we validate totals and choose the output shape that best serves the downstream use.

[pause=1.0]

The teaching database includes several examples because reshaping appears in many domains.

[pause=0.8]

Admissions and sales begin in long form.

[pause=0.7]

Monthly sales and patient metrics begin in wide form.

[pause=0.7]

Survey responses and grades are useful for matrix-style pivots.

[pause=0.7]

The different examples help you focus on the reshape pattern rather than memorizing one dataset.

[pause=1.0]

In long form, the month is stored as a value in a column.

[pause=0.7]

Laptop January and Laptop February occupy different rows.

[pause=0.7]

This shape is flexible because a new month can simply become another row.

[pause=0.7]

Long form is common for time-series analysis, plotting, grouping, and tidy analytical workflows.

[pause=1.0]

In wide form, January and February are separate columns.

[pause=0.7]

Now one row represents a product rather than a product-month.

[pause=0.7]

This can be convenient for scorecards, matrices, and fixed reports.

[pause=0.7]

The same business relationship is being displayed differently, but the row grain has changed.

[pause=1.0]

These two tables represent the same simplified information.

[pause=0.7]

The long table has one product-month per row.

[pause=0.7]

The wide table has one product per row.

[pause=0.7]

Before reshaping, state both grains clearly.

[pause=0.7]

That makes it easier to identify what has changed and whether any information has been aggregated away.

[pause=1.0]

Grain means what one row represents.

[pause=0.7]

A sales fact table may have one row per transaction.

[pause=0.7]

After grouping, the grain may become one product-month.

[pause=0.7]

After pivoting months into columns, the grain may become one product.

[pause=0.7]

If you cannot state the row grain, it is difficult to know whether a reshape is correct.

[pause=1.0]

Before writing a pivot, complete one sentence: one output row represents what?

[pause=0.7]

Once the row meaning is clear, identify which category values should become columns.

[pause=0.7]

Then identify the measure that belongs in each cell.

[pause=0.7]

Finally ask whether several source rows can map to the same cell.

[pause=0.7]

If they can, you need an aggregation rule.

[pause=1.0]

Long form is often the more flexible analytical shape.

[pause=0.7]

If categories change frequently, new values simply appear in rows.

[pause=0.7]

Long form also works naturally with trend charts, filtering, grouping, and many modeling workflows.

[pause=0.7]

It avoids changing the schema every time a new category appears.

[pause=1.0]

Wide form is useful when categories are stable and users want side-by-side comparison.

[pause=0.7]

A scorecard with January, February, and March columns is easy to scan.

[pause=0.7]

A grade matrix can place courses in fixed columns.

[pause=0.7]

But wide schemas become harder to maintain when categories change frequently.

[pause=1.0]

A pivot often requires aggregation.

[pause=0.7]

If only one source row maps to each output cell, the reshape can preserve that value directly.

[pause=0.7]

But if multiple source rows map to one cell, PostgreSQL needs an aggregate such as SUM, COUNT, MAX, or AVG.

[pause=0.7]

That aggregation changes the level of detail, so it must be chosen deliberately.

[pause=1.0]

Before pivoting admissions, inspect the long source.

[pause=0.8]

Each admission is a row.

[pause=0.7]

Diagnosis is stored as a value, not as a column.

[pause=0.7]

The pivot will create separate diagnosis count columns by month.

[pause=0.7]

Understanding the source grain makes the later GROUP BY easier to interpret.

[pause=1.0]

A pivot can be planned with four decisions.

[pause=0.7]

First, define the output row grain.

[pause=0.7]

Second, identify the category values that should become columns.

[pause=0.7]

Third, choose the measure.

[pause=0.7]

Fourth, choose the aggregate needed to fill each cell.

[pause=0.7]

For the diagnosis example, one output row is one month, the categories are diagnoses, and the measure is admission count.

[pause=1.0]

PostgreSQL does not require a special PIVOT keyword for the core patterns taught here.

[pause=0.7]

You can use conditional aggregation.

[pause=0.7]

One common form is SUM with CASE.

[pause=0.7]

PostgreSQL also supports FILTER on aggregate functions, which can be very readable.

[pause=0.7]

Both approaches use the same underlying idea: one grouped output row with category-specific aggregate columns.

[pause=1.0]

This query groups admissions by month.

[pause=0.8]

Inside each SUM, CASE contributes one when the row matches a selected diagnosis and zero otherwise.

[pause=0.7]

The sum becomes the diagnosis count for that month.

[pause=0.7]

Run the query and verify that each result row represents one month.

[pause=1.0]

In the CASE pivot, each output measure has a different condition.

[pause=0.7]

The GROUP BY defines one output row per month.

[pause=0.7]

Inside that month, each SUM looks only at rows belonging to its diagnosis category.

[pause=0.7]

This separation between row grain and category condition is the core pivot pattern.

[pause=1.0]

PostgreSQL FILTER attaches a condition directly to an aggregate.

[pause=0.7]

COUNT star FILTER where diagnosis equals Pneumonia counts only matching rows.

[pause=0.7]

The query is often easier to scan because the aggregate and its condition appear together.

[pause=0.8]

Run it and compare the result with the CASE version.

[pause=0.8]

The output should express the same business meaning.

[pause=1.0]

CASE and FILTER are two styles for conditional aggregation.

[pause=0.7]

CASE is broadly portable and flexible.

[pause=0.7]

FILTER is particularly readable in PostgreSQL when you want category-specific counts or sums.

[pause=0.7]

Choose the form that is clear for the environment you are using.

[pause=0.7]

The output grain and aggregate meaning matter more than the stylistic choice.

[pause=1.0]

A pivot can aggregate revenue instead of counts.

[pause=0.7]

This query groups by sale month.

[pause=0.8]

Each filtered SUM collects revenue for one product.

[pause=0.7]

The result has one row per month and separate revenue columns for Laptop, Mouse, and Keyboard.

[pause=0.7]

Always identify both the output grain and the measure being aggregated.

[pause=1.0]

Survey data often arrives in long form with one row per respondent-question.

[pause=0.7]

If there is at most one score for each respondent and question, MAX can be used as a convenient aggregate to place that value into the correct column.

[pause=0.7]

The output grain becomes one respondent.

[pause=0.7]

The Q1, Q2, and Q3 categories become columns.

[pause=1.0]

An empty pivot cell should not automatically become zero.

[pause=0.7]

NULL may mean no observation was recorded.

[pause=0.7]

Zero may mean the observation exists and its measured value is zero.

[pause=0.7]

Those are different facts.

[pause=0.7]

Before using ELSE zero or COALESCE, decide what an absent source row means for the analytical question.

[pause=1.0]

This example shows two versions of the same pivot cell.

[pause=0.8]

The first CASE has no ELSE zero, so a missing Q3 response stays NULL.

[pause=0.7]

The second explicitly forces zero.

[pause=0.7]

Run the query and find respondents with no Q3 observation.

[pause=0.8]

Ask whether zero is a real score or simply a convenient placeholder.

[pause=0.7]

That distinction affects later averages and models.

[pause=1.0]

A reshape should be validated.

[pause=0.7]

For additive measures such as revenue, calculate the total from the source.

[pause=0.7]

Then calculate the total represented by the pivot cells.

[pause=0.7]

The totals should agree when the same observations are included.

[pause=0.7]

This simple check catches many grouping and join mistakes.

[pause=1.0]

Now we reverse the direction.

[pause=0.7]

The monthly sales table stores January, February, and March as separate columns.

[pause=0.7]

That is convenient for a fixed report, but less flexible for many analytical tasks.

[pause=0.7]

Unpivoting turns those month columns back into row values.

[pause=1.0]

Unpivoting converts repeated measure columns into rows.

[pause=0.7]

The wide source has one product row with several month columns.

[pause=0.7]

The long result will have a month column and a revenue column.

[pause=0.7]

The row grain changes from one product to one product-month.

[pause=1.0]

UNION ALL is a straightforward unpivot pattern.

[pause=0.7]

Write one SELECT for each source column.

[pause=0.7]

Give each SELECT the same output structure.

[pause=0.7]

Then stack the rows with UNION ALL.

[pause=0.7]

This is verbose but very beginner-friendly because each source column is visible in its own SELECT.

[pause=1.0]

This query produces three SELECT blocks.

[pause=0.8]

Each one assigns a month date and uses the corresponding wide revenue column.

[pause=0.7]

UNION ALL stacks the results.

[pause=0.7]

Run it and verify that one product row has expanded into multiple product-month rows.

[pause=1.0]

PostgreSQL offers a compact unpivot pattern with CROSS JOIN LATERAL and VALUES.

[pause=0.7]

For each monthly sales row, VALUES creates several month-revenue pairs.

[pause=0.7]

LATERAL allows those pairs to reference jan revenue, feb revenue, and mar revenue from the current source row.

[pause=0.7]

This is often cleaner than repeating full SELECT statements.

[pause=1.0]

This query keeps the source table once.

[pause=0.8]

The lateral VALUES block emits three rows for each product.

[pause=0.7]

Each generated row contains a sale month and the corresponding revenue.

[pause=0.7]

Run the query and compare the output with UNION ALL.

[pause=0.8]

The two forms should represent the same long relationship.

[pause=1.0]

Both methods are useful.

[pause=0.7]

UNION ALL is explicit and easy to read when there are only a few columns.

[pause=0.7]

LATERAL VALUES is compact when many columns follow the same repeated structure.

[pause=0.7]

The correct choice is the one that keeps the transformation clear and maintainable.

[pause=1.0]

Patient metrics provides another unpivot example.

[pause=0.8]

Heart rate, systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure, and oxygen saturation are separate wide columns.

[pause=0.7]

The lateral VALUES block converts them into metric and value rows.

[pause=0.7]

This can be useful for generic plotting, rule processing, or feature inspection.

[pause=1.0]

When several source columns become one value column, PostgreSQL needs a common data type.

[pause=0.7]

If one metric is integer and another is numeric, explicit casts may be helpful.

[pause=0.7]

The patient metric example casts selected values to numeric.

[pause=0.8]

Do not let type coercion become an accidental part of the reshape.

[pause=0.7]

Choose the long value type deliberately.

[pause=1.0]

Unpivoting raises a NULL-policy question.

[pause=0.7]

You can preserve rows whose value is NULL.

[pause=0.7]

That keeps the category present and marks the measurement missing.

[pause=0.7]

Or you can drop NULL rows after unpivoting.

[pause=0.7]

The right choice depends on whether missingness itself matters to the analysis.

[pause=1.0]

This query uses the lateral VALUES pattern and then filters out rows whose generated revenue is NULL.

[pause=0.8]

The WHERE clause makes the policy explicit.

[pause=0.7]

Run it and compare the row count with a version that keeps all generated rows.

[pause=0.8]

Always document whether missing cells were preserved or removed.

[pause=1.0]

A reshape round trip is not automatically reversible.

[pause=0.7]

If the pivot aggregated transaction rows to monthly totals, unpivoting can only recover those monthly totals.

[pause=0.7]

It cannot recreate the original transaction IDs or individual amounts.

[pause=0.7]

The grain that survives is the aggregated grain.

[pause=1.0]

This query first creates a wide product-level table with month totals.

[pause=0.8]

Then it unpivots the wide columns into product-month rows.

[pause=0.7]

The result is long again, but it is not the original transaction table.

[pause=0.7]

It is one row per product-month total.

[pause=0.7]

That is the key distinction between reshaping and recovering detail.

[pause=1.0]

A reshape is more reversible when each source value maps cleanly to one output cell and category labels are preserved.

[pause=0.7]

It becomes lossy when several rows are aggregated into one cell.

[pause=0.7]

Dropping NULL rows can also remove missingness information.

[pause=0.7]

Collapsing categories can remove distinctions.

[pause=0.7]

Always identify which information survives the transformation.

[pause=1.0]

The seeded sales table intentionally contains multiple Laptop transactions in January.

[pause=0.7]

A product by month pivot has only one Laptop January cell.

[pause=0.7]

That means the two transaction rows must be combined.

[pause=0.7]

If the measure is revenue, SUM is a reasonable choice.

[pause=0.7]

But the transaction-level detail is no longer present in that cell.

[pause=1.0]

This query groups the sales source by product and month.

[pause=0.8]

COUNT tells us how many transaction rows exist in each product-month group.

[pause=0.7]

SUM shows the total revenue that would fill a pivot cell.

[pause=0.7]

Look for groups where source rows is greater than one.

[pause=0.7]

Those groups prove that the pivot requires aggregation.

[pause=1.0]

The first query shows the individual Laptop January sale rows.

[pause=0.8]

The second query sums them into one product-month value.

[pause=0.8]

That one total can be placed into a pivot cell.

[pause=0.7]

But after aggregation, the individual sale IDs and amounts cannot be recovered from the total alone.

[pause=0.7]

This is the detail lost by aggregation.

[pause=1.0]

Reshaping often happens after joins.

[pause=0.7]

The danger is that a join can multiply fact rows.

[pause=0.7]

If you join a patient dimension to admissions, the admission grain can remain intact.

[pause=0.7]

But joining admissions to another one-to-many child table can create repeated admission combinations.

[pause=0.7]

Always check cardinality before pivoting joined data.

[pause=1.0]

This query starts from patients and left joins admissions.

[pause=0.8]

The patient table contributes one descriptive row per patient.

[pause=0.7]

Admissions provides the events being counted.

[pause=0.7]

Filtered counts create January, February, and March admission columns.

[pause=0.7]

The GROUP BY keeps one output row per patient.

[pause=0.7]

Because the join relationship is understood, the counts remain meaningful.

[pause=1.0]

The important question is whether the join preserves the measure's fact grain.

[pause=0.7]

A many-to-one lookup often preserves the fact rows.

[pause=0.7]

A broad join between two fact-like tables can multiply them.

[pause=0.7]

If rows are already duplicated before the pivot, the pivot aggregates inflated facts.

[pause=0.7]

Check row counts and key relationships first.

[pause=1.0]

Pre-aggregation can help control grain.

[pause=0.7]

First summarize the fact table to the level you actually need.

[pause=0.7]

Then perform later joins or pivots from that stable grain.

[pause=0.7]

This separates fact aggregation from presentation reshaping and can make the query easier to verify.

[pause=1.0]

The CTE first creates one row per product, category, and month.

[pause=0.7]

The outer query then groups by category and creates month columns.

[pause=0.8]

So there are two grain changes.

[pause=0.7]

Run the query and state both of them.

[pause=0.8]

Being explicit about intermediate grain is one of the best protections against accidental double counting.

[pause=1.0]

Wide pivot columns are part of the schema.

[pause=0.7]

If the categories are stable, that is manageable.

[pause=0.7]

If new products or diagnoses appear frequently, the SQL must change to add columns.

[pause=0.7]

Long form handles dynamic categories more naturally because new categories become new rows.

[pause=0.7]

Often a BI tool can create the presentation matrix from long data.

[pause=1.0]

Before creating a static pivot, inspect the category values.

[pause=0.8]

This script lists distinct diagnoses and products.

[pause=0.7]

If the current data includes categories you did not plan for, a fixed pivot may omit them.

[pause=0.7]

Discovery helps make the schema decision explicit.

[pause=1.0]

This static pivot creates three diagnosis columns.

[pause=0.7]

It works well when those categories are intentionally selected and stable.

[pause=0.7]

The advantage is a predictable schema.

[pause=0.7]

The limitation is that any new diagnosis category will not automatically appear as a new column.

[pause=1.0]

PostgreSQL has an optional crosstab function through the tablefunc extension.

[pause=0.7]

It can create pivot tables, but it requires extension support and explicit output-column definitions.

[pause=0.7]

For this course, conditional aggregation is the core pattern because it is transparent and works well in the browser environment.

[pause=0.7]

You can explore crosstab later for selected reporting scenarios.

[pause=1.0]

There is no universally best shape.

[pause=0.7]

A fixed dashboard matrix may be easier to read in wide form.

[pause=0.7]

A trend chart usually benefits from long form because the category and time dimensions stay as values.

[pause=0.7]

Choose the shape based on the next analytical or reporting task.

[pause=1.0]

This query creates a long monthly product summary.

[pause=0.8]

Each row represents one product-month.

[pause=0.7]

The time dimension, category dimension, and measure stay in separate columns.

[pause=0.7]

This shape is flexible for charting because new products become new rows instead of requiring new columns.

[pause=1.0]

Reshaping should be driven by the downstream consumer.

[pause=0.7]

Long form is often more robust for charts, modeling, and changing categories.

[pause=0.7]

Wide form is useful for fixed business reports and interfaces.

[pause=0.7]

A good pipeline can keep a reusable long analytical table and create wide presentation outputs only where needed.

[pause=1.0]

Practice 1 reshapes student grades.

[pause=0.8]

The source is long: one student-course grade per row.

[pause=0.7]

The output should have one row per student and fixed course columns.

[pause=0.7]

A missing course should remain NULL because no recorded grade is not the same as a grade of zero.

[pause=1.0]

This query left joins students to grades and groups by student.

[pause=0.8]

Filtered MAX expressions place each course grade in its own column.

[pause=0.7]

MAX works because the exercise expects at most one grade per student-course.

[pause=0.7]

Run the query and inspect how missing courses remain NULL.

[pause=1.0]

Practice 2 creates a patient-month admission matrix.

[pause=0.8]

The output grain is one row per patient.

[pause=0.7]

Month columns contain admission counts, and total admissions provides an overall measure.

[pause=0.7]

Because the query starts from patients with a left join, patients with no admissions are still represented.

[pause=1.0]

This query creates January, February, and March admission counts plus a total.

[pause=0.8]

The left join preserves patients with no admissions.

[pause=0.7]

Run the query and compare total admissions with the displayed month columns.

[pause=0.8]

If the dataset contains only those months, the totals should align with their sum.

[pause=1.0]

The retail project asks you to build two different outputs from the same facts.

[pause=0.8]

The long table supports trend analysis.

[pause=0.7]

The wide table supports a scorecard.

[pause=0.7]

Both should represent the same revenue at different shapes.

[pause=0.7]

The project is not complete until you compare totals across the source and both reshaped outputs.

[pause=1.0]

A strong reshape project includes validation.

[pause=0.8]

State the grain at every stage.

[pause=0.7]

Compare additive totals.

[pause=0.8]

Document the NULL policy.

[pause=0.7]

Confirm that expected categories and months are present.

[pause=0.7]

These checks make the transformation reproducible and reduce the chance of silent data loss.

[pause=1.0]

Use this checkpoint to test conceptual understanding.

[pause=0.8]

Explain the row grain.

[pause=0.7]

Explain why an aggregate may be required.

[pause=0.7]

Explain the difference between missing and zero.

[pause=0.7]

Explain the common-type requirement for unpivoted values.

[pause=0.7]

And explain why an aggregate pivot-unpivot round trip cannot recreate original transactions.

[pause=1.0]

The applied challenge asks you to reshape the long sales table into one row per product.

[pause=0.7]

Create January, February, and March revenue columns.

[pause=0.7]

Preserve NULL when there is no observation for a product-month.

[pause=0.7]

Then explain why the result has fewer rows than the source.

[pause=0.7]

Do not start with syntax alone. First state the output grain and the measure that belongs in each pivot cell.

[pause=1.0]

These are the key habits from Module 10.

[pause=0.7]

State the grain first.

[pause=0.7]

Use conditional aggregation for pivots.

[pause=0.7]

Use UNION ALL or lateral VALUES for unpivoting.

[pause=0.7]

Protect the distinction between NULL and zero.

[pause=0.7]

Validate totals and row counts.

[pause=0.7]

And choose long or wide form based on the downstream task, not because one format is always better.

[pause=1.0]

Use this guide when deciding how to reshape.

[pause=0.7]

If category values should become columns, pivot with conditional aggregation.

[pause=0.7]

If columns should become rows, use UNION ALL or lateral VALUES.

[pause=0.7]

Keep dynamic categories long when possible.

[pause=0.7]

Use a wide form for stable matrix reporting.

[pause=0.7]

And whenever several source rows map to one cell, make the aggregate decision explicit.

[pause=1.0]

Module 11 builds on the SQL foundations developed so far.

[pause=0.7]

You now have experience with relational design, joins, subqueries, strings and dates, cleaning, and reshaping.

[pause=0.7]

Advanced SQL will combine those ideas into more powerful analytical patterns.

[pause=0.7]

Carry forward the grain habit from this module, because advanced queries are only trustworthy when you know what each row represents.

[pause=1.0]
